title: Using Data to Drive Reliability Investments
situation: At Corellian Freight Analytics, there was no shared sense of what actually deserved engineering time. Whoever had the loudest or most recent outage got the next sprint. Product wanted features, Ops wanted stability, Engineering had more tech debt than capacity to touch it — normal tension, except it was being resolved by whoever argued loudest in the room, not by looking at anything. Real investment decisions — where a quarter of engineering time went — were getting made off anecdotes.
task: Nobody handed this to her — she raised it herself. The task, once Product and Ops leadership agreed it was worth doing: get Product, Ops, and Engineering looking at the same data instead of each defending their own priority from memory. Not "fix reliability" directly — fix how the org decided what to fix. Success meant planning meetings opening with metrics instead of "what feels broken."
action: Partnered with Product and Ops leadership to pick a small set of reliability metrics tied to actual customer experience rather than internal perception — incidents, availability, deployment outcomes, support ticket trends, operational telemetry — and built a shared dashboard off that. Changed the meeting structure so planning stopped opening with "what feels broken" and started with the dashboard on screen. The bigger decision was cultural more than technical: pushed the room to treat anecdotes as hypotheses that still needed the data to back them up, not settled fact — someone could still say "I think X is a problem," it just became the start of a question, not the end of one. Roughly a dozen people across the three groups (three or four engineering leads, a couple from Product, two from Ops) — small enough to get real alignment in a room, not a company-wide rollout. A couple of engineering leads pushed back, since losing "we just had a fire" as an automatic trump card cost them real leverage. Rather than argue them out of it, let the data settle it over a cycle or two — one team's issue turned out real and jumped the line once the numbers backed it; another team's didn't show up in the metrics at all and quietly dropped off.
result: Reliability investment got more focused and predictable across the next few planning cycles — less time spent litigating priorities since the evidence was already shared going in. A handful of recurring issues got fixed while still annoying instead of after becoming customer-facing incidents (no precise before/after number — this is reconstructed from memory and she won't claim false precision on it). The bigger shift: the culture moved. People started asking "what do the metrics say" before proposing a fix, across Eng, Product, and Ops — the part that mattered most and the part with no single number attached. Unexpected cost: real short-term goodwill spent before it paid off — a couple of the pushback leads stayed annoyed for a while, since "the data will vindicate you eventually, maybe" is a hard sell in the moment. In hindsight, she'd bring the skeptical leads into picking the metrics earlier rather than presenting the dashboard once it already existed — would have cost less trust upfront instead of spending a couple of cycles rebuilding it.
raw_transcript:
Q: Set the scene — what was the state of things before this started?
A: No shared sense of what deserved engineering time; loudest/most recent outage won the next sprint; investment decisions were being made off anecdotes, not evidence.

Q: What was your specific responsibility — handed to you or self-initiated?
A: Self-initiated, raised it with Product and Ops leadership. Task was to get everyone looking at the same data instead of defending priorities from memory. Success = planning meetings opening with metrics, not "what feels broken."

Q: Walk me through what you actually did. Room size? Pushback?
A: Picked a small set of customer-facing reliability metrics, built a shared dashboard, changed how planning meetings opened, reframed anecdotes as hypotheses needing data. ~12 people across 3 groups (3-4 eng leads, 2 Product, 2 Ops). Pushback from leads who'd been getting sprint time off recent outages — let the data settle it over a cycle or two rather than arguing in the room.

Q: What changed? Numbers, timelines, reactions? Anything unexpected or you'd do differently?
A: More focused/predictable reliability investment, fewer recurring issues escalating; culture shift toward metrics-first proposals (no clean number on either — old, reconstructed from memory). Unexpected: real short-term goodwill cost with the pushback leads. Would bring skeptics into picking the metrics earlier next time.
notes: Metric-light by design — she explicitly declined to assert precise before/after numbers on a 2019-2021 memory, consistent with her stated standing offer on metric provenance. The Result section's honesty about cost (goodwill spent before it paid off) and the 'what I'd do differently' answer are the richest material here for interview prep.
